## Psalm 70 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview / Superscription

**"For the choirmaster. Of David. To bring remembrance."**

Psalm 70 is almost identical to Psalm 40:13–17, with a few deliberate alterations. Most commentators regard it as a detached fragment of Psalm 40, likely separated for liturgical use. The superscription "to bring remembrance" (Hebrew *lehazkir*) may indicate it was to be used in connection with offerings (cf. 1 Chronicles 16:4) or as a "memorial" to put the Lord in remembrance of the petitioner's request.
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-70.html
— Constable's Notes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-70.html (search excerpt)

Spurgeon called it "the poor man's memorial" and noted that it acts as a connecting link between Psalms 69 and 71, forming "a precious triad of song."
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

Martin Luther reportedly valued this psalm highly: "This prayer is the shield, spear, thunderbolt and defense against every attack of fear, presumption [and] lukewarmness."
— Enduring Word (citing Boice citing Luther): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

Gill notes Jewish interpretive traditions: Kimchi thought it was composed when David fled from Saul or Absalom; the Targum paraphrased "to bring to remembrance" as "to remember the use of the frankincense" (alluding to Leviticus 2:2); Jarchi says it signifies prayer.
— Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/70.htm

The psalm belongs to the "Elohistic Psalter" (Psalms 42–72), where the divine name Elohim generally replaces Yahweh — though this psalm makes the change inconsistently.
— Expositor's Bible Commentary (search excerpt): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-70.html

---

### v. 1: *"Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me!"*

David opens with an urgent, almost breathless cry. In the Hebrew, Spurgeon says, it is "an abrupt and broken cry, O God, to deliver me; O Lord, to help me hasten." The verb "be pleased" found in Psalm 40:13 is missing here, giving the verse added urgency. David asked for haste because delayed deliverance was no help at all.
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

David repeats his request, shifting from "God" (Elohim) to "LORD" (Yahweh), the covenant name. Guzik notes that "by the additional name he hoped to secure additional speed in the reply."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

G. Campbell Morgan observed that such prayers reveal "a mistaken conception of God. God never needs to be called upon to hasten. He is never tarrying uselessly or carelessly." Yet Morgan insisted God still welcomes such imperfect prayers: "He will understand, and in His understanding, interpret our faulty terms by His own perfect knowledge, and give us His best answers to our deepest need."
— Enduring Word (citing Morgan): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

Clarke adds simply: "I am in extreme distress, and the most imminent danger. Haste to help me, or I am lost."
— Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-70.html

Spurgeon comments: "It is not forbidden us, in hours of dire distress, to ask for speed on God's part in his coming to rescue us."
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

---

### v. 2: *"May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; may those who wish me harm be repelled and humiliated."*

David prays for his enemies to be turned back and confused. This is an imprecatory prayer, asking God to bring shame on those who sought to shame David. VanGemeren (cited in Enduring Word) notes: "The psalmist prays for his enemies' fall and shame in accordance with the principles of justice and with the promise of God to curse those who cursed his own."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

Spurgeon observes that the words "together" and "to destroy it" from Psalm 40:14 are omitted here: "a man in haste uses no more words than are actually necessary."
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

The Pulpit Commentary notes the same omissions.
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-70.html

James Montgomery Boice (cited in Enduring Word) offers a pastoral insight: "The kindest thing we can pray for people who do wrong is that their plans will fail, for it may be that in their frustration they will see the folly and true end of evil and be reached for God."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

---

### v. 3: *"May those who say, 'Aha, aha!' retreat because of their shame."*

The cry "Aha, aha!" expresses scornful, gloating mockery. Adam Clarke calls it "a note of supreme contempt." It was bad enough that David's enemies sought his life; they added public ridicule.
— Enduring Word (citing Clarke): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

The Pulpit Commentary notes a textual difference from Psalm 40:15: where Psalm 40 has "Let them be desolate," Psalm 70 has "Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame." The Pulpit Commentary judges this difference "seems to arise from a corruption." The Expositor's Bible Commentary suggests the change may have been an "artistic variation" or perhaps "a slip of memory."
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-70.html
— Expositor's Bible Commentary (search excerpt): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-70.html

Spurgeon wonders if the milder language ("turned back" vs. "desolate") reflects a mellowing with age: "Had growing years matured and mellowed the psalmist's spirit?" Yet he adds that "disappointed malice is the nearest akin to desolation that can well be conceived."
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

Spurgeon also provides a Christological application: the enemies' "Aha, aha!" prefigures the taunts hurled at Christ. James Frame (cited by Spurgeon) writes that "the prescient Saviour would, no doubt, catch in his ears the distant mutter of all the violent and ruthless exclamations with which his foes were about to rend the air."
— Spurgeon (citing Frame): https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

---

### v. 4: *"May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You; may those who love Your salvation always say, 'Let God be magnified!'"*

In the middle of his desperate plea, David pivots to pray for the joy of all God's people. This makes the psalm remarkable: surrounded by enemies and urgent need, David does not pray only for himself but for the whole community of faith.

Stephen Witmer (Desiring God) calls this "nothing short of miraculous — David, in his foxhole, under heavy fire, prays not simply for personal escape, but for gladness among all God's people, and for the continual glorifying of God." He draws a "Christian Hedonist" application: "Christian Hedonism is as much for bleak days as it is for bright ones."
— Desiring God: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/finding-joy-in-the-dark

On "Let God be magnified": David Guzik explains that magnification does not make an object bigger — we cannot make God bigger — but "to magnify something or someone is to perceive it as bigger, and we must do that regarding God."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

Spurgeon provides several rich notes. On those who "love Your salvation," he cites James Frame: "All men are lovers as well as seekers; for all men love. Some love money more than God's salvation; others love pleasure…" On "Let God be magnified," Spurgeon says: "It does not say, let God be magnified by me if he will please to make me successful in business… but it leaves it open. Only let God be magnified, and he may do what he wills with me." Spurgeon also prays ecumenically: "My heart says, 'Let God be magnified among the Wesleyans! The Lord be magnified among the Independents! The Lord be magnified among the Episcopalians! The Lord be magnified among the Baptists!'"
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

Augustine (cited in Spurgeon) expands on the theme: whether one is a sinner confessing, a justified believer, or one who perseveres — in every state the cry is "Be the Lord magnified," not oneself, for "in him was something, in me nothing."
— Spurgeon (citing Augustine): https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

---

### v. 5: *"But I am poor and needy; hurry to me, O God. You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay."*

David returns to his urgent plea, bookending the psalm with the same cry for haste. He combines honest acknowledgment of his poverty with complete dependence on God alone.

**"Poor and needy"**: Clarke renders the Hebrew *ani ve'evyon* as "I am a poor man, and a beggar — an afflicted beggar; a sense of my poverty causes me to beg."
— Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-70.html

Spurgeon notes that Psalm 40:17 has "yet the Lord thinketh upon me" instead of "make haste unto me." The change is deliberate: "Psalm 40 sings of God's thoughts, and, therefore, ends therewith; but the peculiar note of Psalm 70 is 'Make haste,' and, therefore, so it concludes."
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

The Pulpit Commentary agrees this change "cannot be ascribed to a corruption, but must be an alteration made deliberately." The Expositor's Bible Commentary says this change "is like the subtle alteration which a painter might make on his picture by taking out one spot of high light. The gleam of confidence is changed to a call of need, and the tone of the whole psalm is thereby made more plaintive."
— Pulpit Commentary: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-70.html
— Expositor's Bible Commentary (search excerpt): https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-70.html

F. B. Meyer (cited in Enduring Word) offers comfort for those waiting: "But God is making haste. On the wings of every hour, quicker than light leaps from world to world, He is on his way. Delays are not denials, but are necessary to the perfecting of his arrangements."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

Spurgeon adds a congregational application: "We are praying for a display of the Holy Spirit's power in this church, and, in order to have successful pleading in this matter, it is necessary that we should unanimously make the confession of our text, 'I am poor and needy.' We must own that we are powerless in this business."
— Enduring Word (citing Spurgeon): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

Horne (cited in Enduring Word) summarizes: "With such a Father and such a Friend, poverty becometh rich, and weakness itself is strong."
— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

---

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives

Since Psalm 70 is very short and largely duplicates Psalm 40:13–17, most Protestant traditions do not produce distinctly separate teaching on it. What follows is drawn from what I was able to find; where traditions could not be located, this is noted.

### Baptist (Spurgeon)
Spurgeon's treatment (above) is the most extensive traditional Baptist resource. His distinctive emphases include: (a) a strong Christological reading — seeing David's enemies as types of Christ's mockers; (b) combining the language of "poor and needy" with prayer for revival and the Spirit's power in the church; (c) an ecumenical impulse in calling for God to be magnified across all denominations. 
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

### Reformed Baptist / "Christian Hedonism" (Desiring God)
Stephen Witmer's article is the most distinctly tradition-specific take. He reads Psalm 70:4 through the lens of "Christian Hedonism" — the teaching (associated with John Piper) that God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him. Witmer's emphasis is that David pursues joy in God *in the midst* of suffering, not after it. "Don't wait to pursue your joy in God until God has healed your brokenness."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/finding-joy-in-the-dark

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik's notes (above) are thorough and pastoral. His distinctives include: (a) an emphasis on the raw honesty and urgency of prayer as a model for believers; (b) drawing on G. Campbell Morgan to affirm that God accepts even theologically "imperfect" prayers; (c) practical application about praying with more urgency. Guzik is broadly evangelical and does not press distinctively Pentecostal doctrines in this psalm.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-70/

### Catholic and Orthodox
I was unable to retrieve pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org for Psalm 70. Augustine's homily on the verse is preserved in Spurgeon's Treasury, where Augustine treats "poor and needy" as the ongoing state of the believer who still hungers and thirsts after righteousness (citing Matthew 5:6 and Romans 7:23).
— https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps070.php

### Modern Scholarship
I was unable to retrieve the netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org pages. However, the Expositor's Bible Commentary (search excerpt) addresses the text-critical question of whether Psalm 70 or Psalm 40 is original: "Hupfeld holds that this psalm is the original, and Psalm 40 a composite; but most commentators agree in regarding this as a fragment of that psalm. The cut has not been very cleanly made; for the necessary verb 'be pleased' has been left behind, and the symmetry of Psalm 70:1 is destroyed for want of it. The awkward incompleteness of this beginning witnesses that the psalm is a fragment."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-70.html
